core: What pseudocode is: an informal, language-agnostic, high-level description of an algorithm written for humans
Common conventions: uppercase keywords, assignment operator, IF/ELSE selection, WHILE/FOR/REPEAT loops, INPUT/OUTPUT, indentation for blocks
Why pseudocode is used: to design and communicate logic before committing to a programming language
How pseudocode compares with flowcharts and with real (executable) source code
One small correct worked example (sum of 1..n) and what it computes
supporting: There is no single universal pseudocode standard; textbooks, courses, and exam boards each define a style
The structured constructs pseudocode notates: SEQUENCE, selection (IF-THEN-ELSE, CASE), and iteration (WHILE, FOR, REPEAT-UNTIL)
outOfScope: Deep semantics of variables, conditional statements, and loops (each is its own topic)
The concept of an algorithm itself beyond a one-line definition (own topic)

claims.claim: Pseudocode is a kind of structured English for describing algorithms that lets the designer focus on logic without being distracted by language syntax; it is read by people, not by a computer.
There is no universal industry standard for pseudocode; each textbook and each designer may use their own style, so conventions are adopted for consistency rather than being formally mandated.
Pseudocode notates a small set of structured-programming constructs: SEQUENCE, WHILE, IF-THEN-ELSE, REPEAT-UNTIL, FOR, and CASE, which can be nested inside one another.
In common academic conventions the assignment operator is a left arrow ('<identifier> ← <value>'), storing the evaluated right-hand value into the variable on the left.

Common pseudocode conventions write keywords in upper case (IF, WHILE, FOR, REPEAT, PROCEDURE), use indentation to show that statements are contained within a construct, and use INPUT/OUTPUT commands for reading and displaying values.

A pre-condition WHILE loop tests its condition before the statements run, so the body executes only while the condition is true; IF statements select between alternatives and may include an ELSE clause.
An algorithm is a computable set of steps to achieve a desired result; pseudocode is one notation used to describe an algorithm.
The iterative sum of the integers 1 through 5 is 15, matching the closed form n(n+1)/2 for n = 5 (5*6/2 = 15).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact pseudocode symbols and keywords differ across sources (e.g., some conventions use = or := for assignment; some use ENDIF/ENDWHILE, others use indentation alone).
positions: Cambridge 9618 uses ← for assignment and explicit ENDIF/ENDWHILE/NEXT terminators.
Cal Poly's standard treats pseudocode as non-rigorous structured English with recommended (not mandatory) formatting.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented pseudocode as a family of conventions rather than one fixed syntax; used the widely taught ← assignment and uppercase-keyword style while stating explicitly that no universal standard exists.
